---
title: "Glossary"
---

Terms used across the workshop, defined once, in the order you meet them. Each entry
says what the object is, how to think about it as an engineer, and where it is first
built. Module pages link here the first time they use a term.

## The objects of inference

### Model

A joint probability distribution $p(x, \theta)$ over data $x$ and unknowns $\theta$,
written as a generative story: first draw $\theta$ from the prior, then draw $x$ given
$\theta$ from the likelihood. Everything in the workshop starts from a model written
this way. Built from first principles in [Module 2b](../day0/m02b-foundations.qmd).

### Prior

$p(\theta)$: what is plausible for the unknowns before seeing the data. For an engineer
the closest familiar object is a regulariser: a Gaussian prior on regression weights is
L2 regularisation, and the maximum of the posterior is the regularised fit. The prior
also sets the scale on which the data will be weighed.

### Likelihood

$p(x \mid \theta)$ viewed as a function of $\theta$ for the observed $x$. It scores how
well each setting of the unknowns explains the data. It is not a density in $\theta$ and
need not integrate to one.

### Posterior

$p(\theta \mid x)$: what is plausible for the unknowns after seeing the data. By the
product rule, $p(\theta \mid x) = p(x \mid \theta)\,p(\theta) / p(x)$. The posterior is
the object every method in this workshop approximates. Its normaliser is the evidence.

### Evidence (marginal likelihood)

$p(x) = \int p(x \mid \theta)\,p(\theta)\,\dd\theta$: the probability of the data under
the whole model, averaging over the unknowns. It normalises the posterior and scores
models against each other. It is an integral over every unknown at once, which is why it
is usually intractable. The log evidence is the quantity the ELBO lower-bounds.

### Posterior expectation

$\E_{p(\theta \mid x)}[f(\theta)]$ for some function $f$: a posterior mean, a predictive
probability, the probability that one variant beats another. Almost every question you
ask a Bayesian model is an expectation of this form. Approximate inference is the art of
estimating such expectations when the posterior has no closed form.

### Posterior predictive

$p(x_{\text{new}} \mid x) = \int p(x_{\text{new}} \mid \theta)\,p(\theta \mid x)\,\dd\theta$:
the distribution of future data, averaging the likelihood over what you still do not
know about $\theta$. Wider than any single-$\theta$ prediction.

### Change of variables and the Jacobian {#jacobian}

If $x = f(z)$ for an invertible map $f$, then $\log p_z(z) = \log p_x(f(z)) + \log|\det J_f(z)|$:
the density in the new coordinates is the old density at the mapped point, times how
much the map stretches a small volume there. Probability mass is conserved; density is
not. The extra term is the log absolute Jacobian, and forgetting it gives a silently
wrong posterior. It appears whenever a constrained parameter (a variance, a
probability) is moved to the real line, and it is the entire mechanism of a normalising
flow. Built from first principles in
[Module 2b](../day0/m02b-foundations.qmd#sec-jacobian), which also provides a
three-line checker (`workshop/jacobian_check.py`) for any transform.

### Conjugacy

A prior family is conjugate to a likelihood if the posterior lies in the same family.
Then inference is exact and reduces to arithmetic on parameters. Rare but important:
it supplies the exact answers that the approximate methods are tested against. Built in
[Module 5](../day1/m05-conjugacy.qmd).

## Exponential families

### Exponential family

A set of densities $p(x \mid \eta) = h(x)\exp(\eta^\top t(x) - A(\eta))$: the log density
is linear in a fixed vector of statistics $t(x)$. Gaussian, Bernoulli, categorical,
gamma, Dirichlet, Poisson and beta are all members. Built in
[Module 3](../day1/m03-expfam-core.qmd).

### Sufficient statistic

$t(x)$: the function of the data through which the likelihood depends on the parameter.
Everything else about the data is irrelevant to the parameter. For a Gaussian with
unknown mean and variance, $t(x) = (x, x^2)$ and only the sums of $x$ and $x^2$ matter.

### Natural parameter

$\eta$: the coordinates in which the log density is linear in $t(x)$. Textbook parameters
(mean and variance, probability, shape and rate) are nonlinear reparameterisations of
$\eta$. Products of densities add natural parameters, which is why Bayesian updates
become addition in these coordinates.

### Log-partition function

$A(\eta) = \log\int h(x)\exp(\eta^\top t(x))\,\dd x$: the log of the normalising constant.
Its gradient is the mean of $t(x)$ and its Hessian is the covariance of $t(x)$, so one
function generates moments, Fisher information and KL divergences.

### Mean parameters

$\mu = \E_\eta[t(x)] = \nabla A(\eta)$: the expected sufficient statistics. The second
coordinate system for an exponential family, dual to $\eta$. Variational updates are
often simplest in mean coordinates. Built in [Module 4](../day1/m04-kl-bregman.qmd).

### Fisher information

$F(\eta) = \mathrm{Cov}_\eta[t(x)] = \nabla^2 A(\eta)$: the expected curvature of the
log-likelihood. Large Fisher information means the data pin down $\eta$ precisely. It is
the metric behind natural gradients and the ideal mass matrix for HMC.

### KL divergence

$\KL(p\,\|\,q) = \E_p[\log p(x) - \log q(x)] \ge 0$: how much a code built for $q$ wastes
when the data come from $p$, in nats. Asymmetric. Zero only when $p = q$. The objective
that variational inference minimises, indirectly, through the ELBO.

### Bregman divergence

$D_A(\eta_q, \eta_p) = A(\eta_q) - A(\eta_p) - (\eta_q - \eta_p)^\top\nabla A(\eta_p)$: the
gap between a convex function and its tangent plane. For an exponential family it
equals $\KL(p_{\eta_p}\,\|\,p_{\eta_q})$.

## Variational inference

### Variational family

A set of tractable distributions $q_\phi(\theta)$ indexed by variational parameters
$\phi$, within which we search for the best approximation to the posterior. Mean-field
Gaussians, normalising flows and the encoder of a VAE are all variational families.

### ELBO (evidence lower bound)

$\ELBO(\phi) = \E_{q_\phi}[\log p(x, \theta) - \log q_\phi(\theta)] = \log p(x) - \KL(q_\phi\,\|\,p(\theta\mid x))$.
Maximising it over $\phi$ minimises the KL divergence to the posterior without ever
computing the evidence. Derived in [Module 6](../day2/m06-cavi.qmd).

### Mean-field

A variational family that factorises over the unknowns, $q(\theta) = \prod_i q_i(\theta_i)$.
Cheap, often accurate for means, systematically too narrow for variances because it
cannot represent posterior correlations.

### CAVI (coordinate ascent variational inference)

Optimise the ELBO one factor $q_i$ at a time, each update in closed form for conjugate
models. The ELBO never decreases. Built in [Module 6](../day2/m06-cavi.qmd).

### Score-function (REINFORCE) gradient

An estimator of $\nabla_\phi\E_{q_\phi}[f(\theta)]$ that uses $f$ only through its values:
$\E_{q_\phi}[f(\theta)\nabla_\phi\log q_\phi(\theta)]$. Works for discrete $\theta$ and
black-box $f$; high variance. Built in [Module 7](../day2/m07-gradient-estimators.qmd).

### Reparameterisation (pathwise) gradient

Write $\theta = g_\phi(\varepsilon)$ with $\varepsilon$ parameter-free, then
$\nabla_\phi\E[f(\theta)] = \E[\nabla_\phi f(g_\phi(\varepsilon))]$. Uses $\nabla f$, so
much lower variance; needs a differentiable $f$ and a reparameterisable $q$.

### Stochastic variational inference

Optimise the ELBO with noisy gradients from Monte Carlo samples of $q$ and minibatches
of data. The engine of modern VI. Built in [Module 8](../day2/m08-bbvi-engine.qmd).

### Bijector

A smooth invertible map with a computable log-determinant of its Jacobian. Used to move
constrained parameters (a variance, a probability) to the whole real line so Gaussians
and gradient methods apply, and as the building block of normalising flows.

### Amortised inference

Instead of fitting variational parameters per data point, learn a function (an encoder)
from data to variational parameters. The VAE encoder is amortised inference. Built in
[Module 14](../day4/m14-vae.qmd).

## Markov chain Monte Carlo

### Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)

Construct a random walk whose long-run distribution is the posterior, then average the
visited points. Exact in the limit, with no family restriction; the price is correlated
samples and the need for diagnostics.

### Detailed balance

$p(\theta)\,K(\theta \to \theta') = p(\theta')\,K(\theta' \to \theta)$ for a transition
kernel $K$: the condition that makes a chain leave the posterior invariant. The
Metropolis acceptance rule is the standard way to enforce it.

### Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC)

Introduce an auxiliary momentum, simulate frictionless motion on the negative log
posterior with a symplectic integrator, and accept or reject the endpoint. Moves far
with high acceptance. Built in [Module 9](../day3/m09-hmc-core.qmd).

### Leapfrog integrator

The second-order, reversible, volume-preserving integrator used by HMC. Its energy error
is bounded over long trajectories, which keeps acceptance high.

### Step size and mass matrix

The two tunables of HMC. The step size trades accuracy for speed; the mass matrix
rescales coordinates so the posterior looks round. Adapted automatically in
[Module 10](../day3/m10-adaptation.qmd).

### Divergence

A trajectory whose energy error blows up, indicating a region the integrator cannot
follow, usually a sharp funnel. A diagnostic, not a numerical accident.

### $\hat R$ and effective sample size

$\hat R$ compares between-chain and within-chain variance; values well above 1 mean the
chains disagree. Effective sample size converts correlated draws into the number of
independent draws they are worth. Built in [Module 11](../day3/m11-diagnostics.qmd).

## Probabilistic programming

### Trace

The record of every random choice a model made during one execution: name,
distribution, value, whether it was observed. The data structure on which inference
algorithms operate. Built in [Module 12](../day4/m12-effect-handlers.qmd).

### Effect handler

A context manager that intercepts `sample` calls and changes what they do: record, replay,
condition on data, fix values. Composing handlers is how one model definition serves
many inference algorithms.

### Guide

The probabilistic-programming word for a variational family: a program with the same
sample sites as the model but with learnable parameters.

## Capstone

### Normalising flow

A sequence of bijectors applied to a simple base distribution; the density of the
output is computed exactly by the change-of-variables formula. An expressive
variational family. Built in [Track A](../day5/m15a-flows.qmd).

### Score function (of a density)

$\nabla_x \log p(x)$, the gradient of the log density with respect to the data, not the
parameters. Diffusion models learn it at every noise level. Built in
[Track B](../day5/m15b-diffusion.qmd).

### Structural causal model

Each variable is a deterministic function of its parents and an independent noise term.
Interventions replace a function; counterfactuals re-run the model with the noise
inferred from an observed outcome. Built in [Track C](../day5/m15c-scm.qmd).

## Notation that changes meaning between days {#notation}

The workshop follows each field's standard notation rather than inventing a uniform
one, so a few letters are reused. Each page says which reading applies.

| Symbol | Days 1, 2, 4 and Track A | Day 3 | Track B |
|---|---|---|---|
| $q$ | the variational distribution $q_\phi(\theta)$ | the position coordinate in HMC, $(q, p)$ | the forward (noising) process $q(x_t \mid x_0)$ |
| $p$ | the model or target density | the momentum in HMC | the model density $p_t$ |
| $\theta$ | the unknowns being inferred | also the unknowns; written $q$ inside the sampler | the score-network weights |
| score | $\nabla_\phi \log q_\phi(z)$, gradient in the *parameters* (Module 7) | not used | $\nabla_x \log p_t(x)$, gradient in the *data point* |
| $x$ | observed data | observed data | the data point being noised, $x_t$ |
| $\eta$ | natural parameters of an exponential family | the standardised deviations $\eta_j$ of the non-centred model | not used |

The clash in $q$ is the one that bites. On Day 3, $q$ is where the particle is and $p$
is how fast it is going, because that is how every HMC paper writes Hamilton's
equations; the posterior is then $\pi(q)$. When Module 11 compares HMC against VI,
the variational distribution is written $q_\phi$ with the subscript to tell them apart.
